# Catalogue

26 generative patterns across 7 categories, and 7 advisory entries that answer with what to write instead.

Every generative entry is emitted as complete TypeScript files that have been typechecked and whose generated tests have been executed. This page is a reference to read before installing anything; `patterns describe <name>` is the authority on what a given pattern accepts, and cannot go stale.

- **Type safety** — [branded-type](#branded-type), [discriminated-union](#discriminated-union), [parse-dont-validate](#parse-dont-validate), [result](#result), [typestate](#typestate)
- **Async resilience** — [async-queue](#async-queue), [circuit-breaker](#circuit-breaker), [debounce](#debounce), [retry](#retry), [semaphore](#semaphore), [token-bucket](#token-bucket)
- **LLM orchestration** — [chat-model-port](#chat-model-port), [context-budget](#context-budget), [model-middleware](#model-middleware), [stream-accumulator](#stream-accumulator), [structured-output](#structured-output), [tool-loop](#tool-loop)
- **Data access** — [repository](#repository), [unit-of-work](#unit-of-work)
- **Structural** — [adapter](#adapter), [decorator](#decorator), [gateway](#gateway)
- **Behavioural** — [specification](#specification), [typed-emitter](#typed-emitter)
- **Creational** — [builder](#builder), [factory](#factory)
- **[Advisory](#advisory-entries)** — iterator, observer, prototype, singleton, strategy, template-method, visitor

## Type safety

### branded-type

**Branded Primitive.** Give a primitive a nominal identity, so a value of one meaning cannot be passed where another is wanted, while it stays usable everywhere the primitive is.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the value being branded, so that it stops being interchangeable with every other value of the same primitive type).

**Options**

- `base` — `string` | `number`, default `string`. The primitive underneath. `string` is the identifier case, where the mistake being prevented is passing one entity's id where another's is wanted — two arguments of the same type in the same order, which no test reliably catches. `number` carries a defect the string case does not: arithmetic silently discards the brand, so adding two quantities produces a plain number and assigning it back has to be rejected. That is the property most worth seeing before relying on a branded number, because it means every derived value needs an explicit trip back through the constructor. The choice also names the artefact — an identifier and a quantity are different types with different files — so switching it is a rename rather than an edit.
- `construction` — `assert` | `result` | `cast`, default `assert`. How a value gets in, which is where a brand is kept honest or quietly given up. `assert` throws on a value that breaks the rule, which suits a boundary that has already decided bad input is exceptional. `result` returns the failure as a value, for a boundary that has to report several problems or answer without throwing. `cast` emits no rule at all and only the conspicuously named unchecked constructor, which is the honest rendering for a value already valid by construction elsewhere — a key read back from a database — where inventing a validation rule would be theatre.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the executable suite and the compile-time suite alongside the implementation. The guarantee itself is pinned in the example either way, since a type-level claim left unasserted is not a guarantee.

Related: `discriminated-union`, `parse-dont-validate`, `result`, `typestate`.

### discriminated-union

**Discriminated Union.** Model a value that is exactly one of several shapes, so that illegal combinations cannot be constructed and a shape added later cannot be silently left unhandled.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the union being declared, whose members share a discriminant).

**Options**

- `dispatch` — `switch` | `record`, default `switch`. How a caller handles every case, and where exhaustiveness is enforced. `switch` is flow-based: narrowing happens per branch and completeness is established by handing the value to a function taking `never` in the default, which fails to compile once a member is unhandled. `record` is structural: handlers arrive as an object keyed by the discriminant, so a missing key is a compile error at every call site without anyone remembering to add a check. The difference matters when a member is added — the `switch` form is only as good as the default branch each author wrote, while the record form cannot be written incompletely in the first place.
- `guards` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit a named type predicate per member, for narrowing outside a dispatch — filtering a list, or checking one case at a boundary. Worth more than it appears, because of a conflict that is easy to miss: the compiler now infers a predicate from an unannotated function whose body narrows, so `filter((e) => e.kind === "shipped")` does narrow — but writing the return type as `: boolean`, which most explicit-return-type lint rules require, silently opts out and leaves the elements unnarrowed. An explicit `event is OrderShipped` satisfies both, states the claim rather than leaving it to be inferred, and can be reused by name.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the executable suite and the compile-time suite alongside the implementation. Exhaustiveness is pinned in the example either way, since it is the guarantee the pattern exists for.

Related: `branded-type`, `result`, `specification`, `typestate`.

### parse-dont-validate

**Parse, Don't Validate.** Turn unknown input into a type only a successful check could have produced, so that what the check learned is carried in the type rather than discarded at the next function boundary.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the type the parser produces from untrusted input).

Writes `FirstLine`, `Id` itself, so an identifier cannot be one of those in any casing.

**Options**

- `errors` — `first` | `all`, default `all`. What a failure reports. `first` stops at the problem it meets, which is the right answer for an internal boundary where any bad input is a bug and the first one names it. `all` visits every field and returns them together, which is what an API boundary needs, because a caller made to fix one field per round trip will make several and a form can only mark up problems it was told about. The difference is not cosmetic: accumulating requires every parser to be run rather than short-circuited, and the failure to carry a list rather than a value.
- `combinators` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit a composable parser kit — a `Parser<T>` type with leaf parsers and combinators over it — rather than one hand-written function that checks each field in sequence. The kit costs an abstraction to learn and repays it twice: paths compose automatically, so a problem inside an array element reports `lines[1]` without anyone threading a prefix through by hand, and the parsed type is *derived from the parser* rather than declared next to it, which removes the possibility of the two drifting apart. Straight-line parsing is the honest choice for a single small boundary, where the kit is more machinery than the problem deserves.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the executable suite and the compile-time suite alongside the implementation. The claim that a check cannot substitute for a parse is pinned in the example either way, since it is the reason the pattern exists.

Related: `branded-type`, `result`, `typestate`.

### result

**Result Type.** Model an operation's failure as a value in its return type instead of a thrown exception.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the value a successful result carries).

**Options**

- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.
- `includeAsync` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the async combinators (fromPromise, mapAsync, andThenAsync) in addition to the synchronous surface.
- `includeCollections` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the collection combinators (all, partition) that turn many results into one.

### typestate

**Typestate.** Put an object's state in its type, so that an operation belonging to another state is not callable rather than merely documented as an error.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the type whose legal transitions are being encoded).

Writes `Equal`, `Expect`, `NotAssignable` itself, so an identifier cannot be one of those in any casing.

**Options**

- `representation` — `parameterised` | `distinct`, default `parameterised`. Where the state lives. `parameterised` is one class carrying the state as a type argument, with each operation constrained by a `this` parameter, which buys method syntax, a fluent chain that reads as the workflow, and functions generic over any state. `distinct` is one type per state with free functions between them, which is plainer, needs no class, and survives a round trip through JSON. The difference that should decide it is not syntax: a private constructor makes the parameterised states unreachable except through the transitions, whereas plain interfaces can be fabricated by any object literal, so the distinct form guards the operations without guarding the states themselves.
- `staleGuard` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Reject a value whose transition has already been taken. This exists because of a limit that cannot be engineered away: TypeScript has no linear types, so a transition consuming a value cannot stop the caller from using that same value again — `order.submit()` twice is not a compile error, and both calls return something the types are perfectly happy with. Turn this off only where every value is threaded through a chain and never bound to a name, since that is the sole discipline the compiler will not check for you.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the executable suite and the compile-time suite alongside the implementation. What each state forbids is pinned in the example either way, since that is the guarantee the pattern exists for.

Related: `branded-type`, `builder`, `discriminated-union`, `parse-dont-validate`.

## Async resilience

### async-queue

**Bounded Work Queue.** Take ownership of submitted work, run a fixed number of items at once, and let the caller bound the backlog, reorder it, wait for it to drain, or be told when an item fails.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the unit of work the queue carries).

**Options**

- `ordering` — `fifo` | `priority`, default `fifo`. The order waiting work is started in. `fifo` is arrival order and needs no per-task argument. `priority` accepts a number per task and starts the highest first, breaking ties by arrival so that equal-priority work is still first-in-first-out — the tie-break is explicit rather than left to a sort being stable, because "stable" is a property of the sort and not of the queue, and nobody reading the code would think to check it. Note what priority costs: strictly ordered, low-priority work is starved for as long as higher-priority work keeps arriving.
- `bounded` — `true` | `false`, default `false`. Whether the backlog has a limit. Unbounded, a producer faster than the workers turns the queue into an unbounded buffer, and the failure is a heap that grows until the process is killed with no indication of which queue did it. Bounded, submission past the limit is refused with a named error, so overload is a handled outcome at the point of submission; a `whenSpace` promise is emitted alongside it for producers that would rather wait than shed.
- `failures` — `promise` | `sink`, default `promise`. Where a task's error goes. `promise` is ordinary promise behaviour — it arrives at whoever awaits what was submitted — and suits a queue whose results are collected. It has one consequence worth stating plainly: on Node an unawaited rejection terminates the process, so submitting fire-and-forget work under this setting means one failing task takes the process with it. `sink` takes a handler at construction, reports every failure to it exactly once, and marks the returned promise as handled so that discarding it is safe; that is the setting for a queue used as a background worker.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `semaphore`, `retry`, `circuit-breaker`.

### circuit-breaker

**Circuit Breaker.** Stop calling a dependency that is failing, and probe it occasionally to find out when it has recovered.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the dependency the breaker protects).

**Options**

- `failureCounting` — `consecutive` | `rolling-window`, default `consecutive`. What counts as enough failure to open. `consecutive` opens after a run of failures with no success between them, and forgets the run on any success. `rolling-window` opens when enough failures land inside a time window, so an intermittent fault that never quite manages a clean run still trips it.
- `halfOpen` — `single-probe` | `sampled`, default `single-probe`. How recovery is tested once the cooldown expires. `single-probe` admits exactly one call and decides on it alone. `sampled` admits several and requires a quota of successes, which is slower to close but far less likely to close onto a dependency that is only intermittently back.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `retry`.

### debounce

**Debounced Call.** Collapse a burst of calls into one, with the timer injected so it can be driven rather than waited for, and without starving a caller who never stops calling.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the operation being debounced).

**Options**

- `edge` — `trailing` | `leading` | `both`, default `trailing`. Which end of the burst invokes. `trailing` waits for quiet and is what a search-as-you-type wants: nothing happens until the typing stops. `leading` acts on the first call and drops the rest of the burst, which is what a submit button wants, since the response to a click must not wait. `both` acts immediately and again at the end if anything else arrived — and carries the defect worth generating around: a single call must invoke once, not twice, which every naive implementation of it gets wrong. Encoded as three values rather than two booleans so that "neither edge", which never invokes at all, cannot be asked for.
- `result` — `promise` | `void`, default `promise`. What a caller gets back. `promise` settles every caller in a burst with the outcome of the invocation their call caused, which is the answer a debounced fetch needs and the one an implementation returning the previous result cannot give. `void` returns nothing and takes a required error handler instead, because a call whose result is discarded still has a failure that has to go somewhere — and on Node an unhandled rejection ends the process. That is the same fork as `failures` on `async-queue`, for the same reason.
- `maxWait` — `true` | `false`, default `false`. Whether to enforce a ceiling on the delay. Without one, a caller who never goes quiet for a whole wait is never served at all — the failure a plain debounce has and the reason this option exists. It brings its own trap: the ceiling must not be restarted by later calls, or neither timer ever expires and the ceiling silently does nothing, and it must be re-armed from its own expiry rather than from the next call, or the interval it promises drifts by the gap between calls.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `async-queue`, `semaphore`, `retry`.

### retry

**Retry with Backoff.** Re-attempt a failing asynchronous operation on a bounded, jittered schedule so a transient fault does not become a request failure.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the operation being retried).

**Options**

- `backoff` — `exponential` | `linear` | `constant`, default `exponential`. How the delay grows between attempts. `exponential` multiplies by a factor each time, `linear` adds the base delay each time, `constant` waits the same amount every time.
- `jitter` — `full` | `equal` | `none`, default `full`. How much randomness to mix into each delay, so that many clients failing together do not retry in lockstep. `full` picks anywhere from zero to the computed delay, `equal` picks from the upper half of it, `none` uses it exactly and needs no random source.
- `cancellation` — `abort-signal` | `none`, default `abort-signal`. Whether the retry loop accepts an AbortSignal, so a caller can abandon it mid-wait. `none` emits a loop with no cancellation plumbing at all.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `circuit-breaker`.

### semaphore

**Bounded Concurrency Semaphore.** Hold the number of operations running at once to a fixed limit, queueing the rest in arrival order, without leaking a permit when one of them fails or is abandoned.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the resource whose concurrency is being limited).

**Options**

- `cancellation` — `abort-signal` | `none`, default `abort-signal`. Whether a caller can abandon a wait. `abort-signal` accepts a signal, removes the waiter from the queue when it fires, and hands on a permit that arrives for a waiter already gone — the race that turns a cancellable limiter into a stalled one. `none` emits a semaphore whose waiters cannot be withdrawn, and therefore no queue-removal path to get wrong.
- `weighted` — `true` | `false`, default `false`. Whether a caller may take more than one permit at a time, for a limit that is a budget rather than a count — bytes in flight rather than requests. Weights change the fairness rule: a lighter waiter behind a heavier one must not be served first, or the heavy one starves under sustained load, so the queue head blocks. Off, every waiter takes one permit and the head can never block.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `circuit-breaker`, `retry`.

### token-bucket

**Token Bucket Rate Limit.** Allow a burst up to a capacity and a sustained rate beyond it, with the level derived from elapsed time rather than refilled by a timer.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the operation the bucket rate-limits).

**Options**

- `waiting` — `refuse` | `wait`, default `refuse`. What happens when there are not enough tokens. `refuse` reports it and returns, which is what a server deciding whether to answer with 429 needs: it must not hold the request open, and it wants the retry delay to send back. `wait` queues the caller until the tokens exist, which is what a client calling someone else's rate-limited API needs, since the work has to happen and waiting is cheaper than being rejected. The queue brings everything a queue brings — arrival order, no barging by a caller who wants less, and cancellation — so the two renderings are genuinely different artefacts rather than one with a flag.
- `keyed` — `true` | `false`, default `false`. Whether there is one bucket or one per subject. Almost every real limit is per-user, per-tenant or per-address, and the naive way to get there is a map that is never emptied — a memory leak whose growth is controlled by whoever is sending the traffic, which makes it a denial-of-service vector rather than merely untidy. Keyed emits the eviction that fixes it, and it is exact rather than approximate: a bucket refilled to capacity is indistinguishable from one that never existed, so it can be dropped without changing any answer the limiter would give.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `debounce`, `semaphore`, `async-queue`, `retry`.

## LLM orchestration

### chat-model-port

**Chat Model Port.** Depend on one small interface for a chat model instead of on a provider's SDK, with the wire format behind an adapter that a recorded body can test.

**Reaches the network.** The emitted factory wires encode and decode to fetch. Both of those are pure functions over plain data, so the generated tests replay recorded bodies through an injected transport and never open a socket; pass your own fetch to record, replay, or add a header. Substitute at `fetch`, and left alone it talks to `The selected provider's documented endpoint, overridable with baseUrl.`.

**Options**

- `provider` — `openai-chat` | `anthropic-messages`, default `openai-chat`. Which wire format the adapter speaks. `openai-chat` is the chat-completions shape, which many services other than OpenAI also accept — a system prompt as the first message, one message per tool result, and tool arguments as a JSON string. `anthropic-messages` is the Messages shape — a system prompt as a top-level field, a required output limit, content as blocks, tool results inside a user turn, and tool input as a value. Both adapters implement the same port, which is the point: the differences are absorbed in one file each rather than spread through the code that calls them. The adapter is named for the format it speaks, so two of them can sit beside one port without colliding.
- `streaming` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Whether the port declares `stream` and the adapter can decode a server-sent event stream. Turning it off removes the stream part union, the event framing, the byte-stream bridge, and the per-format event decoding — worth doing for a caller who only ever waits for a whole answer, and worth keeping for anyone showing output as it arrives, since the framing is where a hand-written reader goes wrong.
- `emitScope` — `full` | `core-only` | `binding-only`, default `full`. Which half of the pattern to emit. `full` is both. `core-only` is the port and the provider-independent machinery, with an example and suite that demonstrate it against a model written by hand rather than against a wire format this scope did not emit. `binding-only` is one adapter — for a project that already has the port, and which then requires `coreModule`. A second provider is a second `binding-only` request against the same core.
- `coreModule` — string, default —. Where the already-installed port lives, as the adapter should import it: `./chat-model-port.js` beside the adapter, `../lib/chat-model-port.js` when it sits in another directory, or a package name. Required by `binding-only` and meaningless otherwise, since a full bundle carries the port beside the adapter and imports it as a sibling.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. Worth keeping here more than in most patterns: the encoder and the decoder are pure functions over recorded bodies, so the suite is the only thing standing between a wire-format detail and a failure that only appears against the live service.

Related: `adapter`, `gateway`, `parse-dont-validate`, `retry`.

### context-budget

**Context Budget.** Fit a conversation into a model's context window before sending it, with the answer's room reserved and the turns that cannot be dropped named.

**Options**

- `strategy` — `drop-oldest` | `summarise` | `middle-out`, default `drop-oldest`. Which turns lose. `drop-oldest` keeps the newest turns that fit and stops at the first one that does not, rather than stepping over it to fit a smaller turn from behind it — a conversation with a hole in it reads to the model as though those turns never happened. `summarise` makes the same choice and folds what it dropped into one message, whose cost is reserved *before* the choice rather than discovered after it, because a summary is not free and a request that overflows by exactly the size of its summary is a hard failure to read. `middle-out` keeps the oldest turns as well as the newest, on the grounds that the task was usually stated first; it needs a `reserveForHead`, and it leaves the gap unannounced — which is the trade against `summarise`.
- `toolPairing` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Treat an assistant turn that called tools and the tool results answering it as one unit, kept or dropped whole. This is the rule a hand-written sliding window breaks: drop the assistant turn and keep the results and the request is rejected because a `toolCallId` refers to nothing; keep the turn and drop the results and it is rejected for the call nobody answered. Neither is a truncation bug the caller can see coming, because the window arithmetic was right. Off, the message union has no tool role in it at all, so a conversation carrying tool results cannot be passed in the first place.
- `onOverflow` — `refuse` | `throw`, default `refuse`. What happens when even the messages that cannot be dropped do not fit — a system prompt plus a question larger than the window. `refuse` returns the arm that says so, carrying the two numbers a caller needs to report it; `throw` raises an error carrying the same two, for a call site that has no branch to put them in. Neither shortens the question's text: a truncated question is a different question, and answering that is worse than declining.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. Costs are counted by an injected function, so the suite pins the arithmetic exactly rather than approximately: that the reply's room comes out of the window before anything is measured, that a system prompt and the newest turn survive a window two turns wide, that the kept turns are a contiguous run, and that a tool call and its results are never separated.

Related: `chat-model-port`, `tool-loop`, `model-middleware`, `result`.

### model-middleware

**Model Middleware.** Wrap a chat model in layers that see every request and every response, without the caller or the provider learning that they are there.

**Options**

- `streaming` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Whether the seam covers `stream` as well as `generate`, which brings the `wrapStream` hook and the rule that goes with it. Worth keeping for anything that streams, because a layer written only over `generate` is silently absent from a streamed call — the types permit it and nothing at run time complains, which is how a cache appears to work until the day a caller switches to streaming. Turning it off removes the stream half of the seam, so a layer that forgets it cannot be written in the first place.
- `caching` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the caching layer. Keyed on everything in a request that decides its answer — the messages, the tools, the settings — and refusing to cache a request whose `temperature` asks for a different answer each time, which is the check that separates a cache from a bug. Under `streaming` it buffers the parts and replays them, since an `AsyncIterable` is consumed once and a cache that hands the same one back twice yields nothing the second time. Nothing in a request says which model it was going to be sent to, so a store shared between two models needs a `namespace` for each; without one they answer for each other.
- `fallback` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the fallback layer: a second model that answers when the first cannot. This is the layer that only exists at this seam — a provider outage is not something the code calling the model can route around, and a middleware holding the substitute is the one place the choice is invisible from both sides. It declines to substitute for a failure a second provider would repeat, and under `streaming` it will not switch once a part has been handed over, because a caller that has already rendered half an answer cannot be given a different one.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. The model is a function returning a recorded answer, so the suite is cheap and covers what a hand-written chain gets wrong: the order the layers see a request against the order they see the answer, a layer that changes the request for one call and not for the next, a stream that must not be started until it is read from, and a cache asked the same thing twice.

Related: `chat-model-port`, `decorator`, `retry`, `circuit-breaker`.

### stream-accumulator

**Stream Accumulator.** Fold a streamed turn back into a whole one, with each tool call's input assembled from the JSON fragments it arrived in.

**Options**

- `truncation` — `refuse` | `report`, default `refuse`. What a stream that stopped early is. `refuse` throws, with the partial turn attached to the error, so a caller cannot mistake a cut-off answer for a finished one — the safe default, because a turn whose stop reason was guessed is the kind of thing that surfaces three layers away. `report` returns the turn with `"other"` as its reason and a warning saying what was missing, which is what an interactive reader wants: the text already on their screen is real, and blanking it because the last event never arrived is worse than saying so. Either way a tool call whose input never finished is left out of the content, since a tool run against half its arguments is worse than a tool not run.
- `progress` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the snapshot surface: a `StreamSnapshot` of the turn so far and an `onProgress` callback the fold invokes after every part. Worth keeping for anything with a reader in front of it, and worth removing for a server-side loop that only wants the finished turn. The snapshot hands over the whole text rather than the latest delta so that a render is idempotent, and a tool call's input as the unparsed fragments it is, since a half-arrived object is not an object.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. The fold is a pure function over a list of parts, so the suite is cheap and the cases are the interesting part: interleaved fragments from concurrent calls, a call that never closed, a part after the finish, and a stream replayed from a recorded array.

Related: `chat-model-port`, `parse-dont-validate`, `result`.

### structured-output

**Structured Output.** Get a schema-validated, typed value out of a chat model, with the retry a failed validation earns.

**Options**

- `strategy` — `tool-call` | `response-format` | `prompt`, default `tool-call`. How the model is asked to produce the value, and therefore where the answer is read from. `tool-call` declares one tool and requires it, taking the value from the call's input: the only strategy that works on every mainstream provider, because tool calling is universal where JSON mode is not, and the one that reads no prose at all — an adapter has already turned the wire into a value. `response-format` sends the OpenAI-compatible response-format instruction, which reaches an OpenAI, Azure, Gemini-compatibility or LiteLLM endpoint; it travels in `providerOptions`, since a field only some providers have is not part of the shared request, and a provider that accepts it and ignores it earns a warning rather than a mysterious failure. `prompt` puts the schema in the system prompt and pulls the first JSON value out of whatever comes back, which is what is left for a model with neither capability.
- `onInvalid` — `retry` | `refuse`, default `retry`. What an answer that does not validate is. `retry` sends it back with its problems named — path and message per issue, bounded by `maxAttempts` — which is worth having because most schema failures are a missing field or a number sent as a string, and a model told exactly which path was wrong usually fixes it next time. It also brings the parts that make a loop honest: `attempts` on the result, usage summed across every call rather than the last one, and a correction shaped for the strategy. `refuse` throws on the first failure with the issues and the value attached, which is the right shape when the caller has its own retry policy or when a second call is not worth its latency.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. The model is a function returning a recorded answer, so the suite is cheap and covers the things a hand-written version gets wrong: a brace inside a string, an escaped quote, brackets that balance around invalid JSON, an answer cut off mid-object, and the shape of the correction that follows a wrong one.

Related: `chat-model-port`, `parse-dont-validate`, `result`, `retry`.

### tool-loop

**Tool Loop.** Run the ask-call-answer cycle until the model has an answer, with every way it can end named and a transcript that survives each of them.

**Options**

- `execution` — `parallel` | `sequential`, default `parallel`. How several calls in one turn are run. `parallel` starts them together, which is what the shape of the turn suggests — a model that asks for three lookups at once has said nothing about their order, and running them in series turns one round trip into three. `sequential` runs them in the order the model listed, which is what tools with side effects on shared state want, and what a tool behind a rate limit or a single connection needs. The difference is visible in the emitted suite, which pins the interleaving either way, and it does not change the results the model is sent: those are ordered by the calls, not by which finished first.
- `onToolError` — `report` | `throw`, default `report`. What a tool that threw is, and a name the model made up along with it. `report` sends the failure back as that call's result with `failed: true` and the message as its output, so the model can read what went wrong and try something else — which is what recovers a run whose argument was one field short, and the reason this is the default. `throw` ends the loop with the failure, the call that caused it, and every step taken so far attached, which is what a caller wants when a tool failing means the request is over: no more tokens are spent on a model that cannot succeed. Both treat an unknown tool name the same way as a tool that threw, because that is what it is — a call that cannot be answered.
- `stopConditions` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the composable stopping surface: a `StopCondition` over the steps so far, plus `hasToolCall` for a tool whose answer ends the run, `repeatedCall` for the loop where the model asks the same thing forever, and `tokenBudget` for the one where it does so cheaply enough not to notice. Worth keeping for anything running unattended, since `maxSteps` alone bounds a stuck run only by spending its whole budget first. Turning it off leaves `maxSteps` and the model's own answer as the two ways a run ends, which is all a short scripted loop needs.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. The model is a function returning recorded turns and the tools are functions, so the suite is cheap and covers what a hand-written loop gets wrong: the transcript after a turn with two calls, a result carrying the id of the call it answers, a tool that threw, a name no tool has, and the run that ends because the bound was reached rather than because the model was finished.

Related: `chat-model-port`, `parse-dont-validate`, `result`, `structured-output`.

## Data access

### repository

**Repository.** Put a typed collection interface in front of a datastore, so query and persistence details live behind one seam instead of spreading through the code that uses them.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the entity the repository stores).

Writes `Repository` itself, so an identifier cannot be that name in any casing.

**Options**

- `pagination` — `cursor` | `offset` | `none`, default `cursor`. How `list` returns more records than fit in one response. `cursor` continues from the last record returned, which stays correct while records are inserted. `offset` skips a count and reports the matching total, which is what a numbered pager needs and is only consistent if nothing is inserted between requests. `none` returns every match, which is honest for a collection with a known bound and a liability otherwise.
- `idStyle` — `branded` | `plain`, default `branded`. Whether the entity's key is a distinct type or an alias for `string`. `branded` means one entity's id cannot be passed where another's is expected, at the cost of a factory call to make one. `plain` costs nothing and checks nothing.
- `emitScope` — `full` | `core-only` | `binding-only`, default `full`. Which half of the pattern to emit. `full` is both. `core-only` is the datastore-independent machinery, which every entity's repository shares, with an example and suite that declare a sample binding inline since there is no binding file to import. `binding-only` is one entity's key type, collection, and factory — for a project that already has the core, and which then requires `coreModule`.
- `coreModule` — string, default —. Where the already-installed core lives, as the binding should import it: `./repository-core.js` beside the binding, `../lib/repository-core.js` when it sits in another directory, or a package name. Required by `binding-only` and meaningless otherwise, since a full bundle carries the core beside the binding and imports it as a sibling.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `result`, `specification`.

### unit-of-work

**Unit of Work.** Accumulate every change a business transaction makes and write them in one commit, so a half-applied transaction and a lost update are both structurally impossible.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the aggregate the unit of work commits).

Writes `KeyChangedError`, `NewRecord` itself, so an identifier cannot be one of those in any casing.

**Options**

- `tracking` — `explicit` | `snapshot`, default `explicit`. How a change is noticed. `explicit` gives each tracked record an `update` method taking a patch, so a change cannot be missed and nothing is copied — and the patch type excludes the key, which makes changing a record's identity a compile error. `snapshot` hands back a mutable draft and works out at commit what differs from a copy taken when it was loaded, which is the rendering that can be handed to domain code that mutates plain objects and knows nothing about persistence. Its costs are worth stating: one shallow copy per loaded record, comparison is by field so a nested object mutated in place is not seen (replacing it is), and the key can only be guarded when the commit runs rather than when the line is written.
- `concurrency` — `version` | `none`, default `version`. What happens when two units of work change the same record. `version` requires every record to carry a `version` number, writes each change conditional on the value that was loaded, and fails the whole commit naming the record that moved — which is the only defence available here, since reads happen before the commit and are therefore outside it. `none` is last-write-wins: the second commit silently overwrites the first, which is fine for records with a single writer and a lost update anywhere else. Choosing `version` also takes the field over: it is assigned on insert rather than supplied, and set from the stored value on commit.
- `emitScope` — `full` | `core-only` | `binding-only`, default `full`. Which half of the pattern to emit. `full` is both. `core-only` is the tracking machinery, the store seam and the in-memory store, which every entity shares, with an example and suite that declare a sample collection inline since there is no binding file to import. `binding-only` is one entity's record constraint, collection and typed accessor — for a project that already has the core, and which then requires `coreModule`.
- `coreModule` — string, default —. Where the already-installed core lives, as the binding should import it: `./unit-of-work-core.js` beside the binding, `../lib/unit-of-work-core.js` when it sits in another directory, or a package name. Required by `binding-only` and meaningless otherwise, since a full bundle carries the core beside the binding and imports it as a sibling.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation. Worth keeping here even by the standards of this option elsewhere: almost everything this pattern promises is about what is *not* written — an unchanged record, a record added and then removed, a commit that failed — and none of that is visible in the types.

Related: `repository`, `specification`, `typestate`.

## Structural

### adapter

**Boundary Adapter.** Translate a foreign representation into one this codebase owns, field by field, so a missing mapping is a compile error and a value that cannot be converted is reported with its field.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the type your own code wants, which the adapter produces from the foreign shape).

**Options**

- `direction` — `one-way` | `two-way`, default `one-way`. `one-way` reads a foreign shape into a domain one, which is what a boundary that only loads needs. `two-way` adds the reverse mapping and the methods that use it, for a boundary that also writes — and makes the round trip a property a test can assert.
- `errorMode` — `result` | `throw`, default `result`. How a source that cannot be mapped is reported. `result` returns the failing fields as a value, which is what lets a boundary answer with all of them at once. `throw` raises an error carrying the same list.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `gateway`, `repository`, `result`.

### decorator

**Method Decorator.** Wrap one behaviour around every method of an existing object — timing, logging, authorisation, caching — without touching the object, repeating the wrapper per method, or changing its type.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the interface being decorated).

**Options**

- `dispatch` — `manifest` | `proxy`, default `manifest`. How the methods to wrap are found. An interface has no members at run time, so something has to supply them. `manifest` takes an object naming them, typed so that it must name every one — adding a method to the subject makes the manifest a compile error rather than silently leaving the new method undecorated, which is the failure this pattern exists to prevent. `proxy` needs no list and picks up members added later, at the cost of an exotic object: it defeats shape-based optimisation, and a property whose value happens to be a function is indistinguishable from a method.
- `stacking` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the combinator that applies several decorations to one subject, outermost first. Worth having wherever more than one concern applies, which is usual — timing outside authorisation outside caching — and worth omitting for a single concern, where it is unreachable surface.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `adapter`, `circuit-breaker`, `retry`.

### gateway

**Service Gateway.** Put one typed boundary in front of a remote service, so every call site sees domain outcomes instead of status codes, unvalidated bodies, and network exceptions.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the remote resource the gateway fronts).

**Reaches the network.** Under transport "fetch" the emitted adapter calls fetch. The gateway itself never mentions it: calls go through a transport function, so a test drives the gateway with a literal reply and a project with its own HTTP client keeps it. Under transport "port-only" no adapter is emitted and nothing reaches the network. Substitute at `transport`.

**Options**

- `transport` — `fetch` | `port-only`, default `fetch`. Whether to emit a `fetch`-backed transport alongside the gateway. `port-only` emits the transport type and leaves the implementation to the caller, which is what a project already holding an HTTP client wants. The gateway itself never references `fetch` either way.
- `errorMode` — `result` | `throw`, default `result`. How a call reports failure. `result` returns a value carrying one of the failure kinds, which is what makes exhaustive handling checkable. `throw` raises an error carrying the same failure, for a codebase whose call sites are already written around exceptions.
- `cancellation` — `abort-signal` | `none`, default `abort-signal`. Whether calls accept an AbortSignal and a per-call timeout, composed so that whichever fires first is reported as its own failure kind. `none` emits a gateway with neither, and therefore one that can wait forever.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `circuit-breaker`, `result`, `retry`.

## Behavioural

### specification

**Specification.** Name a business rule as an object that both tests a candidate and describes itself, so rules compose and the same rule can filter in memory or be pushed into a query.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the candidate the rule tests).

Writes `Equal`, `Expect`, `NegationErasesRefinement`, `NotAssignable`, `NumericField`, `RefinedBy`, `UnfilteredDoesNot` itself, so an identifier cannot be one of those in any casing.

**Options**

- `composition` — `fluent` | `free`, default `fluent`. How rules are combined. `fluent` hangs `and`, `or` and `not` off the specification itself, so a composite reads left to right as the rule it encodes and needs nothing imported to extend it. `free` keeps the combinators as standalone functions, which composes better under `reduce` and over an array of rules built at run time, and keeps the specification a plain value rather than something with behaviour attached. Both preserve the type refinement through arbitrarily deep composition, which was checked rather than assumed.
- `translation` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Give every specification a data description of itself alongside its predicate, so a rule can be handed to a datastore instead of applied to everything the datastore returned. This is the difference between this pattern and a named predicate, and it is bought at a price worth stating plainly: the leaves become declarative, built from a field, an operator and a value rather than from an arbitrary function, because a rule expressed as a closure cannot be translated into anything. What that buys back is that the predicate and the query are *derived from one declaration*, so the in-memory answer and the pushed-down answer cannot disagree. Turn it off where the rules are genuinely arbitrary computation and everything is already in memory.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the executable suite and the compile-time suite alongside the implementation. What composition does to the refinement is pinned in the example either way, since a specification that has quietly stopped narrowing behaves identically at run time to one that has not.

Related: `discriminated-union`, `repository`, `result`.

### typed-emitter

**Typed Emitter.** Give an event emitter an event map, so a name that does not exist, a payload of the wrong shape, and a handler with the wrong parameters are all compile errors.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the subject whose events are being declared).

Writes `TypedEmitter` itself, so an identifier cannot be that name in any casing.

**Options**

- `dispatch` — `sync` | `async`, default `sync`. Whether emitting waits for its handlers. `sync` returns nothing and calls each handler in turn, which is what an emitter is usually for: the emitting code announces something and carries on. `async` returns a promise that settles once every handler has, which is the only version that can report a failure in an asynchronous handler or let the emitter apply back-pressure — and it changes every call site, since an un-awaited `emit` becomes a floating promise. Handlers are awaited in registration order rather than together, so that ordering means what it appears to; the parallel alternative is noted where it would go.
- `errors` — `isolate` | `propagate`, default `isolate`. What one failing handler does to the others. `isolate` runs every handler regardless and reports failures to a sink the caller must supply, which is the default because the premise of an emitter is that the emitting code does not know who is listening — letting an unknown subscriber's bug surface inside the code that emitted couples them straight back together, and the remaining subscribers lose an event they had nothing to do with. Requiring the sink is what keeps that from being silent. `propagate` lets the first failure out of `emit`, which is right where the listeners are part of the same unit as the emitter and a failure among them is a failure of the whole operation.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit the executable suite and the compile-time suite alongside the implementation. The refusals — an unknown event, a mistyped payload, a handler whose parameters do not match — are asserted in the example either way, since they are the whole reason to reach for this over an untyped emitter and no suite that runs can check them.

Related: `discriminated-union`, `result`, `semaphore`.

## Creational

### builder

**Stepwise Builder.** Assemble a value a field at a time, so that a half-finished one cannot be mistaken for a finished one and the fields still owed are named where the mistake is made.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the type being built).

**Options**

- `completeness` — `typestate` | `result` | `throw`, default `typestate`. What happens when `build` is reached before every required field is set. `typestate` makes it a compile error naming the fields still owed, which is the version worth generating — the builder's type carries which fields have been supplied. `result` and `throw` check at run time instead, which is what a builder fed from a form or a config file needs, since the fields it will receive are not known statically.
- `collections` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit `add`, which appends to a field whose value is an array and accepts only such a field. Off for a target with no collections, where the method would be unreachable surface.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `factory`, `result`.

### factory

**Typed Factory.** Construct one of several product types from a key, with the key narrowing the return type at compile time and untrusted keys handled at the boundary.

Names it generates around: `entity` (the type the factory produces).

**Options**

- `registration` — `static` | `dynamic`, default `static`. Whether the set of kinds is closed. `static` fixes it at construction, which is the whole compile-time benefit. `dynamic` adds `extend`, returning a new factory whose type is widened by the creators added, so a plugin discovered at run time is still typed.
- `errorMode` — `result` | `throw`, default `result`. How `from` reports a key it does not recognise. `result` returns a value carrying the unknown key and the ones it knows; `throw` raises an error carrying the same. Only `from` can fail — `create` takes a key the compiler has already checked.
- `context` — `true` | `false`, default `false`. Pass a shared context to every creator alongside the input, so creators can reach dependencies without closing over module state.
- `includeTests` — `true` | `false`, default `true`. Emit an executable test suite alongside the implementation.

Related: `result`.

## Advisory entries

These generate nothing, on purpose. TypeScript absorbed the problem each was solving, so asking for one returns the modern construction and why — as a success, not an error.

### iterator

**Iterator.** Use a generator function, or `[Symbol.iterator]()` on the collection itself instead. The language absorbed this one outright. Implementing `[Symbol.iterator]` makes a collection work with `for...of`, spread, destructuring and every function taking an iterable, and a generator writes the traversal as ordinary sequential code with `yield` in place of a hand-maintained cursor — which is the part worth having, because the cursor field is where a hand-written iterator goes wrong when the traversal is recursive. `AsyncIterable` and `for await` cover the streaming case on the same protocol.

```ts
class Tree<T> {
  constructor(private readonly value: T, private readonly children: Tree<T>[] = []) {}

  *[Symbol.iterator](): Generator<T> {
    yield this.value;
    for (const child of this.children) yield* child;
  }
}

const values = [...new Tree(1, [new Tree(2)])];
```

### observer

**Observer.** Use the `typed-emitter` entry in this catalog, or `EventTarget` where the platform's own type is enough instead. The idea has not been superseded — publish and subscribe is as useful as ever — but the 1994 shape has. An `Observer` interface with an `update` method exists because a function could not be passed as a value; in TypeScript the subscriber is a function, so the interface and the classes implementing it are ceremony around a callback. What is worth generating instead is the part the book does not address and that hand-written emitters usually get wrong: an event map that makes an unknown event name and a mistyped payload compile errors, and dispatch that behaves predictably when a handler subscribes or unsubscribes mid-emit. That is `typed-emitter`.

```ts
// The subscriber is a function, so no Observer interface is needed.
const off = orders.on("placed", (order) => void ship(order));
off(); // unsubscribing is the return value, not a second method and a matching identity
```

### prototype

**Prototype.** Use object spread for a shallow copy, or `structuredClone` for a deep one instead. The pattern exists because a language with nominal types and no object literals needs a virtual method to copy an object without naming its class. TypeScript needs neither: spread copies the fields a type declares and is checked against that type, and `structuredClone` — in every runtime this targets — deep-copies a value including Maps, Sets and Dates without the class having to cooperate. A hand-written `clone` in this setting is worse than the built-ins on the axis that matters, which is what happens when a field is added: spread and `structuredClone` carry it automatically, while `clone` keeps compiling and silently stops copying it.

```ts
const draft = { ...template, title: "Second" }; // shallow, and typechecked
const deep = structuredClone(template); // nested Maps, Sets and Dates included
```

### singleton

**Singleton.** Use a module that exports the value instead. An ES module is already a singleton. The runtime evaluates it once per specifier and hands every later importer the same bindings, so single instantiation is a property of the module system rather than something a class has to defend. What the class adds on top is the part that hurts: a private constructor makes the value unconstructable in a test, so the suite that needs a second one for isolation has to reach past the accessor or reset shared state between cases, and the global reachability that made the pattern attractive is what makes those tests order-dependent. Exporting the value keeps the single instance and loses the ceremony; where a test genuinely needs its own, export the factory beside it and let the module hold the default.

```ts
// config.ts — one instance, because the module is evaluated once.
export const config = loadConfig();

// Export the maker too, so a test can build its own without defeating anything.
export function loadConfig(): Config {
  return { retries: 3 };
}
```

### strategy

**Strategy.** Use a function parameter, typed as a function instead. A strategy class with one method is a function that cannot be passed directly. TypeScript has first-class functions and structural typing, so the interchangeable algorithm is a parameter whose type is a signature, and the compiler checks a candidate against it without anyone declaring that they implement anything. Where the choice is made from data at run time — a name from a config file selecting one of several — that is a lookup returning a function, and the entry worth generating is `factory`, whose keyed map narrows the return type to the one the key selects.

```ts
type Compare<T> = (a: T, b: T) => number;

function sortBy<T>(items: readonly T[], compare: Compare<T>): T[] {
  return items.toSorted(compare);
}
```

### template-method

**Template Method.** Use a function that takes the varying steps as arguments instead. Inheritance is being used here as a way to pass functions, and it is the expensive way. A subclass per variation ties the steps to a class hierarchy, makes two variations impossible to combine, and leaves the reader tracing which override runs — while a function taking the steps as parameters states the seams in its signature, lets a caller mix them freely, and needs no subclass to test one step in isolation. Where the wrapping is what varies rather than the steps, the `decorator` entry composes behaviour around a call without a hierarchy either.

```ts
async function withReport<T>(
  work: () => Promise<T>,
  onDone: (outcome: T) => void,
): Promise<T> {
  const outcome = await work();
  onDone(outcome);
  return outcome;
}
```

### visitor

**Visitor.** Use a discriminated union and a `switch` the compiler checks for exhaustiveness instead. The pattern is a workaround for single dispatch. A language that cannot select behaviour on two types at once needs `accept` and a visitor interface to fake it, and the price is that every operation is spread across as many classes as there are node types. TypeScript narrows a union on its discriminant, so the operation is one function with one `switch`, and the guarantee the visitor interface was providing — that no node type is forgotten — is provided instead by a `never`-typed default arm, which is a compile error naming the case that was missed. Generate the `discriminated-union` entry for that arm and the exhaustiveness check.

```ts
type Node = { kind: "literal"; value: number } | { kind: "add"; left: Node; right: Node };

function evaluate(node: Node): number {
  switch (node.kind) {
    case "literal":
      return node.value;
    case "add":
      return evaluate(node.left) + evaluate(node.right);
    default: {
      // A node type added later fails to compile here, naming itself.
      const unhandled: never = node;
      return unhandled;
    }
  }
}
```
